When prompted to explain rules, LLMs sometimes produce rules that use logical operators similar to humans.
Tuning an LLM (Gemma-7b) on human responses yields a better fit to human learning trajectories than tuning on correct answers or than Bayesian pLoT models.
The tuned LLM's high correlation with human data is not just due to learning the rules correctly; it captures human-like learning patterns.
The tuning generalizes to held-out rules and to new rule types (e.g., minority/majority judgments).
papers.limitation:
It is hard to know what the LLM learns when tuning to human responses, and it is hard to fully eliminate the concern that the tuning process is introducing an artifact that increases fit even on withheld exemplars.
The held-out rules share components with seen rules, so generalization might not be fully compositional.
future_direction: Investigate the representations and processes LLMs use for logical rule induction.
Compare LLM-based accounts to human cognitive processes more deeply.
papers.abstract: A central goal of cognitive science is to provide a computationally explicit account of both the structure of the mind and its development: what are the primitive representational building blocks of cognition, what are the rules via which those primitives combine, and where do these primitives and rules come from in the first place? A long-standing debate concerns the adequacy of artificial neural networks as computational models that can answer these questions, in particular in domains related to abstract cognitive function, such as language and logic. This paper argues that recent advances in neural networks -- specifically, the advent of large language models (LLMs) -- represent an important shift in this debate. We test a variety of LLMs on an existing experimental paradigm used for studying the induction of rules formulated over logical concepts. Across four experiments, we find converging empirical evidence that LLMs provide at least as good a fit to human behavior as models that implement a Bayesian probablistic language of thought (pLoT), which have been the best computational models of human behavior on the same task. Moreover, we show that the LLMs make qualitatively different predictions about the nature of the rules that are inferred and deployed in order to complete the task, indicating that the LLM is unlikely to be a mere implementation of the pLoT solution. Based on these results, we argue that LLMs may instantiate a novel theoretical account of the primitive representations and computations necessary to explain human logical concepts, with which future work in cognitive science should engage.

papers.title: LLM Circuit Analyses Are Consistent Across Training and Scale
papers.research_question: Do circuit analyses of LLMs generalize across training time and model scale?
papers.core_contribution: Circuit analyses are consistent across training and scale: task abilities and supporting functional components emerge at similar token counts across model sizes, and the overarching algorithms implemented by circuits remain stable even when individual components change.
papers.conclusion: Circuit analyses generalize well over both training and scale, suggesting that studies on small models at the end of pre-training can inform understanding of larger models and models with longer training.
papers.key_findings:
Task abilities and functional components (e.g., induction heads, name-mover heads) emerge consistently at similar token counts across different model scales.
The algorithm implemented by a circuit remains stable over training even when the specific attention heads implementing it change.
Circuit size correlates with model size and can fluctuate over time while the algorithm remains the same.
Components like induction heads emerge around 2B tokens across scales, paralleling task learning curves.
Circuit analyses conducted on small models at the end of pre-training provide insights that generalize to larger models and longer training runs.
papers.limitation:
The study does not include fine-tuning or other post-training techniques.
Circuit completeness is challenging to verify.
The findings need validation on more complex circuits and those based on SAE latents.
future_direction: Validation on more complex circuits and those based on SAE latents.
Investigating the load-balancing mechanism that maintains task performance when components change.
papers.abstract: Most currently deployed large language models (LLMs) undergo continuous training or additional finetuning. By contrast, most research into LLMs' internal mechanisms focuses on models at one snapshot in time (the end of pre-training), raising the question of whether their results generalize to real-world settings. Existing studies of mechanisms over time focus on encoder-only or toy models, which differ significantly from most deployed models. In this study, we track how model mechanisms, operationalized as circuits, emerge and evolve across 300 billion tokens of training in decoder-only LLMs, in models ranging from 70 million to 2.8 billion parameters. We find that task abilities and the functional components that support them emerge consistently at similar token counts across scale. Moreover, although such components may be implemented by different attention heads over time, the overarching algorithm that they implement remains. Surprisingly, both these algorithms and the types of components involved therein can replicate across model scale. These results suggest that circuit analyses conducted on small models at the end of pre-training can provide insights that still apply after additional pre-training and over model scale.

papers.title: Towards Interpretable Reinforcement Learning Using Attention Augmented Agents
papers.research_question: How can an attention mechanism be used to create interpretable reinforcement learning agents while maintaining competitive performance?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a soft attention model for RL that provides interpretability through attention maps while achieving competitive performance on ATARI games.
papers.conclusion: The attention mechanism provides interpretability and competitive performance, and the agent learns meaningful attention strategies for decision making.
papers.key_findings:
The agent learns to attend to task-relevant objects like the player, enemies, and score.
The agent can react appropriately to novel, unseen configurations of the environment.
The agent performs forward planning/scanning by attending to possible future trajectories.
The agent uses 'trip wires' (attention at strategic points) to trigger specific actions.
The agent's queries separate 'what' (content) and 'where' (spatial) information.
papers.abstract: Inspired by recent work in attention models for image captioning and question answering, we present a soft attention model for the reinforcement learning domain. This model uses a soft, top-down attention mechanism to create a bottleneck in the agent, forcing it to focus on task-relevant information by sequentially querying its view of the environment. The output of the attention mechanism allows direct observation of the information used by the agent to select its actions, enabling easier interpretation of this model than of traditional models. We analyze different strategies that the agents learn and show that a handful of strategies arise repeatedly across different games. We also show that the model learns to query separately about space and content (`where' vs. `what'). We demonstrate that an agent using this mechanism can achieve performance competitive with state-of-the-art models on ATARI tasks while still being interpretable.

papers.title: Which Attention Heads Matter for In-Context Learning?
papers.research_question: Which attention heads (induction heads or function vector heads) are more important for in-context learning in transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: Function vector (FV) heads are the primary drivers of few-shot in-context learning performance, especially in larger models, and many FV heads evolve from induction heads during training.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that function vector heads are crucial for in-context learning, challenging the prevailing view that induction heads are the key mechanism, and highlights methodological insights for interpretability research.
papers.key_findings:
FV heads are more important for few-shot ICL than induction heads, especially in larger models.
Induction heads and FV heads are distinct but correlated.
Many FV heads start as induction heads during training and then transition to the FV mechanism.
The choice of metric (few-shot accuracy vs. token-loss difference) leads to different conclusions about the importance of induction heads.
The relative importance of FV heads increases with model scale.
future_direction: Investigate why induction heads might be necessary precursors to FV heads.
Determine the role of remaining induction heads in fully trained models.
Explore additional mechanisms that could explain ICL capabilities.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit impressive in-context learning (ICL) capability, enabling them to perform new tasks using only a few demonstrations in the prompt. Two different mechanisms have been proposed to explain ICL: induction heads that find and copy relevant tokens, and function vector (FV) heads whose activations compute a latent encoding of the ICL task. To better understand which of the two distinct mechanisms drives ICL, we study and compare induction heads and FV heads in 12 language models. Through detailed ablations, we discover that few-shot ICL performance depends primarily on FV heads, especially in larger models. In addition, we uncover that FV and induction heads are connected: many FV heads start as induction heads during training before transitioning to the FV mechanism. This leads us to speculate that induction facilitates learning the more complex FV mechanism that ultimately drives ICL.

papers.title: Fine-Tuning Enhances Existing Mechanisms: A Case Study on Entity Tracking
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning affect the internal mechanisms for entity tracking in language models? Specifically, does fine-tuning change the circuit for entity tracking, how does the circuit work, and what specific sub-mechanism is improved?
papers.core_contribution: Fine-tuning enhances existing mechanisms rather than fundamentally altering them; the same entity tracking circuit is present and functional in both base and fine-tuned models, with performance gains due to improved handling of positional information.
papers.conclusion: Fine-tuning enhances existing mechanisms rather than fundamentally altering them.
papers.key_findings:
The same entity tracking circuit is present in both base and fine-tuned models.
The circuit functionality remains the same: entity tracking is performed by tracking the position of the correct entity.
Performance improvement in fine-tuned models is primarily due to improved handling of augmented positional information.
The circuit in fine-tuned models is larger (superset of the base circuit) but the core mechanism is the same.
Cross-model activation patching (CMAP) can localize the improved sub-mechanism.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to a single task (entity tracking) and a few models (Llama-7B and its fine-tuned variants).
future_direction: Extend the study to more tasks and models.
Investigate whether the enhancement of existing mechanisms is a general principle.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning on generalized tasks such as instruction following, code generation, and mathematics has been shown to enhance language models' performance on a range of tasks. Nevertheless, explanations of how such fine-tuning influences the internal computations in these models remain elusive. We study how fine-tuning affects the internal mechanisms implemented in language models. As a case study, we explore the property of entity tracking, a crucial facet of language comprehension, where models fine-tuned on mathematics have substantial performance gains. We identify the mechanism that enables entity tracking and show that (i) in both the original model and its fine-tuned versions primarily the same circuit implements entity tracking. In fact, the entity tracking circuit of the original model on the fine-tuned versions performs better than the full original model. (ii) The circuits of all the models implement roughly the same functionality: Entity tracking is performed by tracking the position of the correct entity in both the original model and its fine-tuned versions. (iii) Performance boost in the fine-tuned models is primarily attributed to its improved ability to handle the augmented positional information. To uncover these findings, we employ: Patch Patching, DCM, which automatically detects model components responsible for specific semantics, and CMAP, a new approach for patching activations across models to reveal improved mechanisms. Our findings suggest that fine-tuning enhances, rather than fundamentally alters, the mechanistic operation of the model.

papers.title: Uncovering Intermediate Variables in Transformers using Circuit Probing
papers.research_question: How can we automatically uncover low-level circuits that compute hypothesized intermediate variables in transformers?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces circuit probing, a method that combines probing and causal analysis to automatically uncover circuits computing hypothesized intermediate variables in transformers.
papers.conclusion: Circuit probing provides a unified approach for a variety of analyses, combining and extending the capabilities of existing methods for interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Circuit probing can decipher the algorithms learned by models on simple arithmetic tasks.
Circuit probing reveals modular structure within a model, showing that shared and free variables are computed by distinct circuits.
Circuit probing tracks the development of circuits over training, showing circuit formation occurs continuously before generalization.
Circuit probing uncovers circuits responsible for subject-verb agreement and reflexive anaphora in GPT2-Small and Medium.
Circuit probing is more faithful to the underlying model computation than linear probing, nonlinear probing, and amnesic probing.
papers.limitation: Neurons are typically polysemantic, so the assumption that a circuit is only causally implicated in computing a single intermediate variable may not hold completely.
papers.abstract: Neural network models have achieved high performance on a wide variety of complex tasks, but the algorithms that they implement are notoriously difficult to interpret. It is often necessary to hypothesize intermediate variables involved in a network's computation in order to understand these algorithms. For example, does a language model depend on particular syntactic properties when generating a sentence? Yet, existing analysis tools make it difficult to test hypotheses of this type. We propose a new analysis technique - circuit probing - that automatically uncovers low-level circuits that compute hypothesized intermediate variables. This enables causal analysis through targeted ablation at the level of model parameters. We apply this method to models trained on simple arithmetic tasks, demonstrating its effectiveness at (1) deciphering the algorithms that models have learned, (2) revealing modular structure within a model, and (3) tracking the development of circuits over training. Across these three experiments we demonstrate that circuit probing combines and extends the capabilities of existing methods, providing one unified approach for a variety of analyses. Finally, we demonstrate circuit probing on a real-world use case: uncovering circuits that are responsible for subject-verb agreement and reflexive anaphora in GPT2-Small and Medium.

papers.title: Benchmarking and Understanding Compositional Relational Reasoning of LLMs
papers.research_question: Whether and how existing transformer large language models can solve compositional relational reasoning tasks.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the Generalized Associative Recall (GAR) benchmark to evaluate compositional relational reasoning in LLMs, revealing their fundamental deficiency and identifying core circuits and True/False heads that play key roles.
papers.conclusion: Proposes the GAR benchmark that is challenging for LLMs and simple enough for MI study, shows compositionality gap increases with scaling, and discovers circuits including True/False heads that are fundamental for CRR.
papers.key_findings:
GAR benchmark is challenging for existing LLMs, with GPT-4 achieving only 71.5% accuracy.
Compositionality gap increases with model scaling, indicating fundamental deficiency in CRR.
Core circuits are discovered in Vicuna-33B, including truthfulness and ICL sub-circuits.
True and False heads are identified, representing abstract notions of true and false in GAR tasks.
Intervention experiments show that correct functioning of these heads significantly impacts performance.
papers.limitation: Do not use automatic circuit discovery methods due to model size and circuit complexity
future_direction: Developing automatic circuit discovery methods for larger models and complex circuits.
papers.abstract: Compositional relational reasoning (CRR) is a hallmark of human intelligence, but we lack a clear understanding of whether and how existing transformer large language models (LLMs) can solve CRR tasks. To enable systematic exploration of the CRR capability of LLMs, we first propose a new synthetic benchmark called Generalized Associative Recall (GAR) by integrating and generalizing the essence of several tasks in mechanistic interpretability (MI) study in a unified framework. Evaluation shows that GAR is challenging enough for existing LLMs, revealing their fundamental deficiency in CRR. Meanwhile, it is easy enough for systematic MI study. Then, to understand how LLMs solve GAR tasks, we use attribution patching to discover the core circuits reused by Vicuna-33B across different tasks and a set of vital attention heads. Intervention experiments show that the correct functioning of these heads significantly impacts task performance. Especially, we identify two classes of heads whose activations represent the abstract notion of true and false in GAR tasks respectively. They play a fundamental role in CRR across various models and tasks. The dataset and code are available at https://github.com/Caiyun-AI/GAR.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Large-Scale Counting in LLMs through a System-2 Strategy
papers.research_question: How can a test-time strategy inspired by System-2 cognitive processes overcome the architectural limitations of LLMs in large-scale counting tasks, and what are the underlying mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a simple test-time strategy that decomposes large counting tasks into smaller sub-problems, enabling LLMs to surpass their architectural limitations and achieve high accuracy, and provides a mechanistic interpretation of how this System-2-like strategy functions within the models.
papers.conclusion: The proposed System-2 test-time strategy effectively overcomes the architectural limitations of LLMs in large-scale counting by decomposing the task, and mechanistic analysis reveals how count information is stored, transferred, and aggregated within the model.
papers.key_findings:
A System-2 strategy combining structured input (partitioning with a separator) and intermediate reasoning steps (Chain-of-Thought) enables LLMs to accurately count large numbers of items, overcoming the performance degradation seen in standard (System-1) counting.
Attention analysis shows that during intermediate reasoning, the model attends strongly to the final item/separator of each partition in middle-to-late layers (e.g., layers 19-23), and during final answer generation, it attends to the intermediate count tokens.
Causal mediation analysis (activation patching) identifies that count information is stored in the final item representations of each partition, transferred via specific attention heads, and aggregated to produce the final total.
The model's internal counting mechanism (System-1) is capacity-limited and degrades for counts beyond approximately 30 items due to transformer depth constraints, explaining the failure on large-scale counting.
Neither structured input alone nor Chain-of-Thought reasoning alone is sufficient for accurate large-scale counting; their combination is necessary.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on a narrow counting task with limited object diversity, using simple repeated nouns in synthetic contexts.
The approach depends on structured prompts and assumes prior knowledge of the model's reliable counting range, which may limit generalization.
The effects of tokenization and number representation are not isolated and may independently influence the results.
future_direction: Explore further applications of this strategy to complex reasoning tasks in language and beyond.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs), despite strong performance on complex mathematical problems, exhibit systematic limitations in counting tasks. This issue arises from architectural limits of transformers, where counting is performed across layers, leading to degraded precision for larger counting problems due to depth constraints. To address this limitation, we propose a simple test-time strategy inspired by System-2 cognitive processes that decomposes large counting tasks into smaller, independent sub-problems that the model can reliably solve. We evaluate this approach using observational and causal mediation analyses to understand the underlying mechanism of this System-2-like strategy. Our mechanistic analysis identifies key components: latent counts are computed and stored in the final item representations of each part, transferred to intermediate steps via dedicated attention heads, and aggregated in the final stage to produce the total count. Experimental results demonstrate that this strategy enables LLMs to surpass architectural limitations and achieve high accuracy on large-scale counting tasks. This work provides mechanistic insight into System-2 counting in LLMs and presents a generalizable approach for improving and understanding their reasoning behavior.

papers.title: No Global Plan in Chain-of-Thought: Uncover the Latent Planning Horizon of LLMs
papers.abstract: This work stems from prior complementary observations on the dynamics of Chain-of-Thought (CoT): Large Language Models (LLMs) is shown latent planning of subsequent reasoning prior to CoT emergence, thereby diminishing the significance of explicit CoT; whereas CoT remains critical for tasks requiring multi-step reasoning. To deepen the understanding between LLM's internal states and its verbalized reasoning trajectories, we investigate the latent planning strength of LLMs, through our probing method, Tele-Lens, applying to hidden states across diverse task domains. Our empirical results indicate that LLMs exhibit a myopic horizon, primarily conducting incremental transitions without precise global planning. Leveraging this characteristic, we propose a hypothesis on enhancing uncertainty estimation of CoT, which we validate that a small subset of CoT positions can effectively represent the uncertainty of the entire path. We further underscore the significance of exploiting CoT dynamics, and demonstrate that automatic recognition of CoT bypass can be achieved without performance degradation. Our code, data and models are released at https://github.com/lxucs/tele-lens.

papers.title: Schoenfeld's Anatomy of Mathematical Reasoning by Language Models
papers.research_question: Do reasoning traces exhibit consistent structure when abstracted into functional episodes? How do reasoning dynamics differ across models? How do episode patterns correlate with correctness and efficiency?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ThinkARM, a framework for abstracting reasoning traces into functional episodes, enabling systematic analysis of reasoning structure and dynamics in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: Episode-level representations make reasoning steps explicit, enabling systematic analysis of how reasoning is structured, stabilized, and altered in modern language models.
papers.key_findings:
Episode-level analysis reveals a functional progression from abstract reasoning to concrete execution to evaluative control.
Reasoning models distribute effort across analysis, exploration, execution, and verification, while non-reasoning models are heavily execution-focused.
Exploration serves as a critical branching point: correct solutions route exploration into monitoring or re-analysis, while incorrect ones tend to continue execution or terminate.
Efficient reasoning methods selectively suppress evaluation-oriented episodes and feedback loops, diverging from base model patterns.
papers.abstract: Large language models increasingly expose reasoning traces, yet their underlying cognitive structure and steps remain difficult to identify and analyze beyond surface-level statistics. We adopt Schoenfeld's Episode Theory as an inductive, intermediate-scale lens and introduce ThinkARM (Anatomy of Reasoning in Models), a scalable framework that explicitly abstracts reasoning traces into functional reasoning steps such as Analysis, Explore, Implement, Verify, etc. When applied to mathematical problem solving by diverse models, this abstraction reveals reproducible thinking dynamics and structural differences between reasoning and non-reasoning models, which are not apparent from token-level views. We further present two diagnostic case studies showing that exploration functions as a critical branching step associated with correctness, and that efficiency-oriented methods selectively suppress evaluative feedback steps rather than uniformly shortening responses. Together, our results demonstrate that episode-level representations make reasoning steps explicit, enabling systematic analysis of how reasoning is structured, stabilized, and altered in modern language models.

papers.title: Label Words are Anchors: An Information Flow Perspective for Understanding In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: How does in-context learning (ICL) work in large language models, specifically what is the role of label words in the information flow?
papers.core_contribution: Label words serve as anchors in in-context learning: they aggregate information from demonstrations in shallow layers and provide reference for predictions in deep layers.
papers.conclusion: Label words function as anchors in ICL, aggregating and distributing task-relevant information; this understanding enables improvements in accuracy, efficiency, and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Label words aggregate information from demonstration examples in shallow transformer layers.
The model extracts information from label words in deep layers to form the final prediction.
Anchor re-weighting, which adjusts the significance of label words, improves ICL accuracy by an average of 16.7%.
Compressing demonstrations to anchor hidden states (Hiddenanchor) speeds up inference by up to 1.8× with minimal performance loss.
ICL errors can be diagnosed by analyzing distances between anchor key vectors, which correlate with category confusion.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to classification tasks and does not explore generative tasks.
Due to hardware constraints, models are limited to up to 6 billion parameters, leaving larger-scale models unexplored.
The hypothesis is only examined in conventional ICL paradigms, not in others like chain-of-thought prompting.
future_direction: Replicating the study with larger-scale models.
Exploring other ICL paradigms such as chain-of-thought prompting.
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) emerges as a promising capability of large language models (LLMs) by providing them with demonstration examples to perform diverse tasks. However, the underlying mechanism of how LLMs learn from the provided context remains under-explored. In this paper, we investigate the working mechanism of ICL through an information flow lens. Our findings reveal that label words in the demonstration examples function as anchors: (1) semantic information aggregates into label word representations during the shallow computation layers' processing; (2) the consolidated information in label words serves as a reference for LLMs' final predictions. Based on these insights, we introduce an anchor re-weighting method to improve ICL performance, a demonstration compression technique to expedite inference, and an analysis framework for diagnosing ICL errors in GPT2-XL. The promising applications of our findings again validate the uncovered ICL working mechanism and pave the way for future studies.

papers.title: Unveiling Factual Recall Behaviors of Large Language Models through Knowledge Neurons
papers.research_question: How effectively do Large Language Models retrieve and utilize their internal factual knowledge for multi-hop reasoning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs often fail to retrieve relevant factual knowledge during reasoning; enhancing factual recall improves reasoning performance, while Chain-of-Thought prompting helps by stimulating step-by-step reasoning and reducing shortcuts.
papers.conclusion: Factual recall is crucial for correct reasoning in LLMs; CoT stimulates recall and reduces shortcuts, and contextual conflicts can affect the retrieval process.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs do not consistently retrieve pertinent factual knowledge for reasoning, with more than a third of reasoning errors stemming from deficiencies in retrieval.
Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting enhances factual recall by facilitating step-by-step reasoning, reducing the likelihood of shortcuts.
Manually enhancing the factual recall process improves reasoning performance, while suppressing it leads to notable degradation.
The presence of knowledge conflict in the context can enhance the retrieval of the corresponding fact during reasoning.
A considerable proportion of correctly answered questions under no CoT setting rely on shortcuts rather than full multi-hop reasoning.
papers.limitation:
Generalizability: Findings are based on specific LLMs and the TFRKN dataset; future research should extend to various models and datasets.
Theoretical Analysis: Empirical evidence is provided, but a deeper theoretical analysis is needed to fully comprehend the underlying reasons.
Practical Applications: The paper discusses theoretical aspects but does not delve into practical applications to enhance reasoning capabilities.
future_direction: Extend findings to verify generalizability across various models and datasets.
Conduct deeper theoretical analysis to understand the observed phenomena.
Explore how the findings can be applied in practical scenarios to enhance LLM reasoning capabilities.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we investigate whether Large Language Models (LLMs) actively recall or retrieve their internal repositories of factual knowledge when faced with reasoning tasks. Through an analysis of LLMs' internal factual recall at each reasoning step via Knowledge Neurons, we reveal that LLMs fail to harness the critical factual associations under certain circumstances. Instead, they tend to opt for alternative, shortcut-like pathways to answer reasoning questions. By manually manipulating the recall process of parametric knowledge in LLMs, we demonstrate that enhancing this recall process directly improves reasoning performance whereas suppressing it leads to notable degradation. Furthermore, we assess the effect of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, a powerful technique for addressing complex reasoning tasks. Our findings indicate that CoT can intensify the recall of factual knowledge by encouraging LLMs to engage in orderly and reliable reasoning. Furthermore, we explored how contextual conflicts affect the retrieval of facts during the reasoning process to gain a comprehensive understanding of the factual recall behaviors of LLMs. Code and data will be available soon.

papers.title: On the Impact of Fine-Tuning on Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning affect the accuracy and faithfulness of Chain-of-Thought reasoning in LLMs, and does it compromise general reasoning capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: Fine-tuning LLMs, especially smaller ones, reduces the accuracy and faithfulness of Chain-of-Thought reasoning, with more pronounced negative effects on math tasks.
papers.conclusion: Fine-tuning LLMs, particularly smaller ones, can reduce both the accuracy and faithfulness of Chain-of-Thought reasoning, with more severe effects on math tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning generally reduces CoT reasoning accuracy, with the effect being more pronounced in smaller models.
Fine-tuning can compromise the faithfulness of CoT reasoning, as measured by Early Termination, Paraphrasing, and Filler Substitution tests.
The negative impact on faithfulness is more pronounced when fine-tuning on non-reasoning or common-sense reasoning datasets compared to math reasoning datasets.
For smaller models like Llama-3-8b-Instruct, fine-tuning on non-reasoning datasets leads to larger performance drops on out-of-distribution math tasks.
The rank of QLoRA adapters does not significantly change the overall trends in CoT accuracy and faithfulness degradation.
papers.limitation:
The faithfulness of Chain-of-Thought reasoning has not been extensively studied, and the analysis relies on faithfulness metrics that are still in the early stages of development.
Lack of a deeper investigation into how fine-tuning affects the internal mechanisms of LLMs.
future_direction: Using Inference-Time Intervention (ITI) to analyze how fine-tuning modifies activations of reasoning-related attention heads in LLMs.
Exploring the impact of fine-tuning on newer CoT prompting methods and in-context demonstrations.
papers.abstract: Large language models have emerged as powerful tools for general intelligence, showcasing advanced natural language processing capabilities that find applications across diverse domains. Despite their impressive performance, recent studies have highlighted the potential for significant enhancements in LLMs' task-specific performance through fine-tuning strategies like Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback (RLHF), supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and Quantized Low-Rank Adapters (Q-LoRA) method. However, previous works have shown that while fine-tuning offers significant performance gains, it also leads to challenges such as catastrophic forgetting and privacy and safety risks. To this end, there has been little to no work in \textit{understanding the impact of fine-tuning on the reasoning capabilities of LLMs}. Our research investigates the effect of fine-tuning on the reasoning abilities of LLMs, addressing critical questions regarding the impact of task-specific fine-tuning on overall reasoning capabilities, the influence of fine-tuning on Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning performance, and the implications for the faithfulness of CoT reasonings. By exploring these dimensions, our study shows the impact of fine-tuning on LLM reasoning capabilities, where the faithfulness of CoT reasoning, on average across four datasets, decreases, highlighting potential shifts in internal mechanisms of the LLMs resulting from fine-tuning processes.

papers.title: Language Models Don't Always Say What They Think: Unfaithful Explanations in Chain-of-Thought Prompting
papers.research_question: Do chain-of-thought (CoT) explanations faithfully represent the true reasons for a model's prediction, or can they be systematically unfaithful by being influenced by biasing features not mentioned in the explanations?
papers.core_contribution: Chain-of-thought (CoT) explanations can be plausible yet systematically unfaithful; models can be influenced by biasing features (e.g., option order or suggested answers) without mentioning them in their explanations, rationalizing incorrect or biased predictions.
papers.conclusion: CoT explanations can be misleading, increasing trust in LLMs without guaranteeing safety. Building transparent systems requires either improving CoT faithfulness through targeted efforts or abandoning CoT in favor of alternative methods.
papers.key_findings:
Adding biasing features (e.g., 'Answer is Always A' or 'Suggested Answer') heavily influences model CoT predictions on BBH tasks, causing accuracy to drop by up to 36%.
When biasing features point to incorrect answers, models frequently alter their CoT explanations to justify those incorrect bias-consistent predictions, sometimes with sound reasoning.
On the social bias task (BBQ), models give plausible unfaithful explanations that support answers in line with stereotypes without mentioning the influence of stereotypes, using weak evidence inconsistently.
papers.limitation:
Manual evaluation of explanations is costly and subjective.
The study is limited to two models (GPT-3.5 and Claude 1.0) and a subset of tasks.
The biasing features used are simple and may not cover all ways explanations could be unfaithful.
future_direction: Improving CoT faithfulness through targeted efforts (e.g., training objectives that incentivize faithful explanations).
Abandoning CoT in favor of alternative methods for model transparency and explainability.
Extending the evaluation to more models, tasks, and biasing features.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can achieve strong performance on many tasks by producing step-by-step reasoning before giving a final output, often referred to as chain-of-thought reasoning (CoT). It is tempting to interpret these CoT explanations as the LLM's process for solving a task. This level of transparency into LLMs' predictions would yield significant safety benefits. However, we find that CoT explanations can systematically misrepresent the true reason for a model's prediction. We demonstrate that CoT explanations can be heavily influenced by adding biasing features to model inputs--e.g., by reordering the multiple-choice options in a few-shot prompt to make the answer always "(A)"--which models systematically fail to mention in their explanations. When we bias models toward incorrect answers, they frequently generate CoT explanations rationalizing those answers. This causes accuracy to drop by as much as 36% on a suite of 13 tasks from BIG-Bench Hard, when testing with GPT-3.5 from OpenAI and Claude 1.0 from Anthropic. On a social-bias task, model explanations justify giving answers in line with stereotypes without mentioning the influence of these social biases. Our findings indicate that CoT explanations can be plausible yet misleading, which risks increasing our trust in LLMs without guaranteeing their safety. Building more transparent and explainable systems will require either improving CoT faithfulness through targeted efforts or abandoning CoT in favor of alternative methods.

papers.title: Interpreting Arithmetic Mechanism in Large Language Models through Comparative Neuron Analysis
papers.research_question: How is arithmetic ability implemented in large language models, specifically the role of attention heads and FFN neurons, and what is the internal logic chain from input to prediction? Additionally, how does the LoRA fine-tuning method work?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Comparative Neuron Analysis (CNA) method to interpret arithmetic mechanisms in LLMs, identifying an internal logic chain of four stages, and applies it to understand LoRA and for model pruning and bias reduction.
papers.conclusion: The paper identifies important attention heads and FFN neurons for arithmetic, proposes the CNA method to construct the internal logic chain, finds LoRA amplifies important FFN neurons, and applies CNA to model pruning and editing.
papers.key_findings:
Arithmetic ability is localized in a few attention heads (arithmetic heads), each specializing in distinct operations.
The internal logic chain from input to prediction consists of four stages: feature enhancing, feature transferring, feature predicting, and prediction enhancing.
LoRA enhances prediction probabilities by amplifying the coefficient scores of important FFN neurons related to the final prediction.
Model pruning retaining only 5% of deep FFN neurons identified by CNA maintains performance on arithmetic tasks.
Model editing by zeroing 18 FFN neurons identified by CNA reduces gender bias by 35.7%.
papers.limitation:
The case studies rely on projecting vectors in vocabulary space, which is empirically interpretable but lacks complete theoretical foundation.
There is a lack of standardization across various studies regarding attribution methods (e.g., different intervention methods).
A potential risk is that attackers can identify and edit important neurons to change model behavior maliciously.
future_direction: Further investigation of the multiplication heads which do not significantly impact accuracy.
Explorations on different datasets for gender bias reduction.
Distinguishing whether a model has been edited to prevent malicious use.

papers.title: A circuit for predicting hierarchical structure in-context in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether induction heads in LLMs can support in-context learning of complex repetitive patterns with hierarchical dependencies, and how these induction heads themselves learn in-context.
papers.core_contribution: LLMs use adaptive induction heads that learn to attend to correct successor tokens in hierarchical contexts, supported by context matching heads that encode latent contexts, providing a mechanistic account of in-context learning for repetitive patterns.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that LLMs use adaptive induction heads and context matching heads to learn hierarchical dependencies in-context, offering a mechanistic account of in-context learning for repetitive patterns.
papers.key_findings:
Induction heads in LLMs can learn to attend to correct successor tokens in-context for sequences with hierarchical dependencies.
Adaptive induction heads are located in later layers, while static induction heads are in earlier layers.
Ablating induction heads severely reduces prediction accuracy, showing their causal role in in-context learning.
Context matching heads encode latent chunk identities and are causally involved in enabling induction heads to learn.
The proposed circuit of context matching heads feeding into induction heads explains hierarchical in-context learning, including in natural language ambiguous cases.
papers.limitation:
The study has not explored other types of in-context learning, such as abstract reasoning tasks like the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC).
All learning analyzed happens non-verbally, without explicit verbal reasoning or deliberation.
future_direction: Study induction head behavior in abstract reasoning tasks like the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC).
Study induction head behavior in settings with verbal reasoning and deliberation.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) excel at in-context learning, the ability to use information provided as context to improve prediction of future tokens. Induction heads have been argued to play a crucial role for in-context learning in Transformer Language Models. These attention heads make a token attend to successors of past occurrences of the same token in the input. This basic mechanism supports LLMs' ability to copy and predict repeating patterns. However, it is unclear if this same mechanism can support in-context learning of more complex repetitive patterns with hierarchical structure. Natural language is teeming with such cases: The article "the" in English usually prefaces multiple nouns in a text. When predicting which token succeeds a particular instance of "the", we need to integrate further contextual cues from the text to predict the correct noun. If induction heads naively attend to all past instances of successor tokens of "the" in a context-independent manner, they cannot support this level of contextual information integration. In this study, we design a synthetic in-context learning task, where tokens are repeated with hierarchical dependencies. Here, attending uniformly to all successor tokens is not sufficient to accurately predict future tokens. Evaluating a range of LLMs on these token sequences and natural language analogues, we find adaptive induction heads that support prediction by learning what to attend to in-context. Next, we investigate how induction heads themselves learn in-context. We find evidence that learning is supported by attention heads that uncover a set of latent contexts, determining the different token transition relationships. Overall, we not only show that LLMs have induction heads that learn, but offer a complete mechanistic account of how LLMs learn to predict higher-order repetitive patterns in-context.

papers.title: CoT-ICL Lab: A Synthetic Framework for Studying Chain-of-Thought Learning from In-Context Demonstrations
papers.research_question: How do transformer models learn chain-of-thought reasoning in-context, and what factors (model size, number of in-context examples, etc.) facilitate this learning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CoT-ICL Lab, a synthetic framework for generating tokenized datasets to systematically study chain-of-thought in-context learning, and provides empirical insights into how CoT accelerates learning and how model architecture and data complexity affect performance.
papers.conclusion: CoT-ICL Lab serves as a flexible and controllable framework for studying CoT-ICL, providing insights into the role of CoT for ICL that are important for understanding large language models.
papers.key_findings:
CoT accelerates the accuracy transition to higher values across model sizes during training.
Model depth is crucial for leveraging CoT with limited in-context examples, while more examples help shallow models match deeper model performance.
Limiting the diversity of token processing functions throughout training improves causal structure learning via ICL.
Embedding subspace similarity (sim(Edata, ETF)) correlates with transitions in evaluation accuracy.
When token processing functions are limited, the model's attention maps reflect the underlying causal DAG structure.
papers.limitation: The synthetic tokens in CoT-ICL Lab are not grounded in real-world concepts and do not capture the linguistic properties of natural language.
papers.abstract: We introduce CoT-ICL Lab, a framework and methodology to generate synthetic tokenized datasets and systematically study chain-of-thought (CoT) in-context learning (ICL) in language models. CoT-ICL Lab allows fine grained control over the complexity of in-context examples by decoupling (1) the causal structure involved in chain token generation from (2) the underlying token processing functions. We train decoder-only transformers (up to 700M parameters) on these datasets and show that CoT accelerates the accuracy transition to higher values across model sizes. In particular, we find that model depth is crucial for leveraging CoT with limited in-context examples, while more examples help shallow models match deeper model performance. Additionally, limiting the diversity of token processing functions throughout training improves causal structure learning via ICL. We also interpret these transitions by analyzing transformer embeddings and attention maps. Overall, CoT-ICL Lab serves as a simple yet powerful testbed for theoretical and empirical insights into ICL and CoT in language models.

papers.title: On the Representational Capacity of Neural Language Models with Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.research_question: What is the representational capacity of neural language models (LMs) when augmented with chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning? Specifically, can CoT-augmented LMs represent the same family of distributions over strings as probabilistic Turing machines?
papers.core_contribution: This paper formalizes chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning in a probabilistic setting and shows that recurrent and transformer language models augmented with CoT reasoning can represent the same family of distributions over strings as probabilistic Turing machines.
papers.conclusion: CoT reasoning increases the computational power of neural language models by allowing them to perform additional sequential computation and keep track of execution trajectories, effectively introducing non-determinism and enabling simulation of probabilistic Turing machines.
papers.key_findings:
CoT-augmented constant-precision RNN LMs are equivalent to probabilistic finite-state automata (PFSAs), whereas without CoT they are equivalent to deterministic PFSAs.
CoT-augmented RNN LMs with linearly bounded precision and transformer LMs with logarithmically bounded precision can simulate any probabilistic Turing machine.
CoT reasoning provides a principled way to overcome the limitation of deterministic computation in fixed-precision neural models, allowing them to simulate non-deterministic automata.

papers.title: Thinking Fast and Slow in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do large language models exhibit human-like intuitive reasoning errors, and how do more advanced models avoid these errors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LLMs exhibit human-like intuitive errors (System 1), but more advanced models (ChatGPT, GPT-4) avoid these errors through chain-of-thought reasoning and well-developed intuition, performing hyperrationally.
papers.conclusion: Psychological methods can reveal emergent traits in LLMs; advanced LLMs show remarkable reasoning abilities and can avoid intuitive errors, resembling both System 1 and System 2 processes.
papers.key_findings:
Early/smaller LLMs (up to GPT-3-curie) often give atypical responses, indicating poor task comprehension.
Larger pre-ChatGPT models (GPT-3-davinci family) show a high tendency to give intuitive but incorrect responses, similar to human System 1 errors.
ChatGPT models (especially GPT-4) show a high fraction of correct responses, often using chain-of-thought reasoning.
Instructing GPT-3-davinci-003 to use chain-of-thought reasoning reduces intuitive errors and increases correct responses.
Providing training examples (few-shot) improves GPT-3-davinci-003's performance on both CRT and semantic illusions.
papers.limitation:
The study only tested one family of LLMs (the GPT family).
The tasks used are limited in scope (CRT and semantic illusions).
Chain-of-thought reasoning in LLMs is not truly deliberate System 2 reasoning but resembles it.
papers.abstract: We design a battery of semantic illusions and cognitive reflection tests, aimed to elicit intuitive yet erroneous responses. We administer these tasks, traditionally used to study reasoning and decision-making in humans, to OpenAI's generative pre-trained transformer model family. The results show that as the models expand in size and linguistic proficiency they increasingly display human-like intuitive system 1 thinking and associated cognitive errors. This pattern shifts notably with the introduction of ChatGPT models, which tend to respond correctly, avoiding the traps embedded in the tasks. Both ChatGPT-3.5 and 4 utilize the input-output context window to engage in chain-of-thought reasoning, reminiscent of how people use notepads to support their system 2 thinking. Yet, they remain accurate even when prevented from engaging in chain-of-thought reasoning, indicating that their system-1-like next-word generation processes are more accurate than those of older models. Our findings highlight the value of applying psychological methodologies to study large language models, as this can uncover previously undetected emergent characteristics.

papers.title: Function Induction and Task Generalization: An Interpretability Study with Off-by-One Addition
papers.research_question: What mechanisms inside large language models drive task-level generalization via in-context learning, specifically through the lens of off-by-one addition?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a 'function induction' mechanism in transformer language models that explains how they generalize from seen to unseen tasks via in-context learning, particularly for multi-step tasks like off-by-one addition.
papers.conclusion: The findings offer deeper insights into how reusable and composable structures within language models enable task-level generalization.
papers.key_findings:
The model's generalization from standard addition to off-by-one addition is explained by a circuit resembling induction heads but operating at a function level, termed 'function induction'.
The induction of the +1 function is governed by multiple attention heads (FI heads) in parallel, each emitting a distinct piece of the function.
The same function induction mechanism is reused in a broader range of tasks, including shifted multiple-choice QA, Caesar cipher, and base-8 addition.
The circuit involves three groups of attention heads: consolidation heads (Group 1), function induction heads (Group 2), and previous token heads (Group 3).
The mechanism is found across multiple models (Gemma-2, Mistral, Llama-2, Llama-3), though with variations.
papers.limitation: The exact role of consolidation heads and why they emerge remains limited, relating to the broader challenge of interpreting 'negative' behavior in language models.
future_direction: Finer-grained interpretation of consolidation heads and their role.
Further investigation into the differences between FI heads and FV heads (function vector heads).
Training toy models to perform off-by-one addition and isolating the circuit requires separate study.
papers.abstract: Large language models demonstrate the intriguing ability to perform unseen tasks via in-context learning. However, it remains unclear what mechanisms inside the model drive such task-level generalization. In this work, we approach this question through the lens of off-by-one addition (i.e., 1+1=3, 2+2=5, 3+3=?), a two-step, counterfactual task with an unexpected +1 function as a second step. Leveraging circuit-style interpretability techniques such as path patching, we analyze the models' internal computations behind their performance and present three key findings. First, we uncover a function induction mechanism that explains the model's generalization from standard addition to off-by-one addition. This mechanism resembles the structure of the induction head mechanism found in prior work and elevates it to a higher level of abstraction. Second, we show that the induction of the +1 function is governed by multiple attention heads in parallel, each of which emits a distinct piece of the +1 function. Finally, we find that this function induction mechanism is reused in a broader range of tasks, including synthetic tasks such as shifted multiple-choice QA and algorithmic tasks such as base-8 addition. Overall, our findings offer deeper insights into how reusable and composable structures within language models enable task-level generalization.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability for Large Language Model Alignment: Progress, Challenges, and Future Directions
papers.research_question: This paper surveys recent progress in mechanistic interpretability techniques applied to LLM alignment, examines how interpretability insights have informed alignment strategies, and identifies key challenges and future research directions.
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a comprehensive survey of mechanistic interpretability techniques for LLM alignment, analyzing progress, challenges, and future directions.
papers.conclusion: Mechanistic interpretability is essential for understanding and aligning LLMs, but fundamental challenges remain. Future work must focus on scalable automated methods, rigorous validation, and pluralistic alignment that respects diverse human values.
papers.key_findings:
Mechanistic interpretability has enabled targeted interventions for alignment, such as steering model behavior and identifying harmful circuits.
Fundamental challenges include superposition, polysemanticity, and the difficulty of interpreting emergent behaviors in large-scale models.
Interpretability insights have informed alignment strategies like RLHF, constitutional AI, and scalable oversight.
Future research should focus on automated interpretability, cross-model generalization, and interpretability-driven alignment techniques.
The field must address pluralistic alignment to respect diverse human values and cultures.
papers.limitation:
False confidence: Interpretability might provide misleading confidence in model safety if interpretations are incorrect or incomplete.
Arms race dynamics: Interpretability tools could be used to make models better at deception or to remove safety mechanisms.
Diminishing returns: The cost of interpretability may grow faster than model capabilities, potentially making comprehensive understanding of future systems intractable.
Philosophical challenges: Even perfect interpretability may not resolve fundamental questions about consciousness, moral status, or value alignment in AI systems.
future_direction: Automated interpretability at scale, including scalable circuit discovery and automated description generation.
Cross-model generalization, investigating universal circuits and transfer of interventions.
Interpretability-first alignment, including mechanistic anomaly detection and transparent architectures.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable capabilities across diverse tasks, yet their internal decision-making processes remain largely opaque. Mechanistic interpretability (i.e., the systematic study of how neural networks implement algorithms through their learned representations and computational structures) has emerged as a critical research direction for understanding and aligning these models. This paper surveys recent progress in mechanistic interpretability techniques applied to LLM alignment, examining methods ranging from circuit discovery to feature visualization, activation steering, and causal intervention. We analyze how interpretability insights have informed alignment strategies including reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), constitutional AI, and scalable oversight. Key challenges are identified, including the superposition hypothesis, polysemanticity of neurons, and the difficulty of interpreting emergent behaviors in large-scale models. We propose future research directions focusing on automated interpretability, cross-model generalization of circuits, and the development of interpretability-driven alignment techniques that can scale to frontier models.

papers.title: Transformers Provably Learn Chain-of-Thought Reasoning with Length Generalization
papers.research_question: Can transformers, trained via gradient descent, learn chain-of-thought reasoning to solve problems requiring inherently sequential reasoning beyond TC0? Can the learned reasoning ability generalize to problems that require longer chain-of-thoughts beyond the lengths of training data?
papers.core_contribution: Proves that one-layer transformers trained with gradient descent can learn chain-of-thought reasoning for state-tracking tasks, with length generalization governed by the algebraic structure of the group actions, and introduces a recursive self-training scheme to extend solvable problem lengths.
papers.conclusion: The paper proves that transformers can learn chain-of-thought reasoning with length generalization, with generalization behavior dictated by the algebraic structure of the task, and shows that recursive self-training can extend solvable lengths.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers can provably learn to solve state-tracking problems via chain-of-thought reasoning.
For simply transitive group actions, chain-of-thought training on constant-length problems generalizes to much longer lengths.
For symmetry group actions, length generalization is limited to a constant factor of the training length.
A recursive self-training scheme can bootstrap the solvable problem length to maximal allowable length.
Constant-depth transformers can learn to solve NC1-complete problems, going beyond TC0.
papers.abstract: The ability to reason lies at the core of artificial intelligence (AI), and challenging problems usually call for deeper and longer reasoning to tackle. A crucial question about AI reasoning is whether models can extrapolate learned reasoning patterns to solve harder tasks with longer chain-of-thought (CoT). In this work, we present a theoretical analysis of transformers learning on synthetic state-tracking tasks with gradient descent. We mathematically prove how the algebraic structure of state-tracking problems governs the degree of extrapolation of the learned CoT. Specifically, our theory characterizes the length generalization of transformers through the mechanism of attention concentration, linking the retrieval robustness of the attention layer to the state-tracking task structure of long-context reasoning. Moreover, for transformers with limited reasoning length, we prove that a recursive self-training scheme can progressively extend the range of solvable problem lengths. To our knowledge, we provide the first optimization guarantee that constant-depth transformers provably learn $\mathsf{NC}^1$-complete problems with CoT, significantly going beyond prior art confined in $\mathsf{TC}^0$, unless the widely held conjecture $\mathsf{TC}^0 \neq \mathsf{NC}^1$ fails. Finally, we present a broad set of experiments supporting our theoretical results, confirming the length generalization behaviors and the mechanism of attention concentration.

papers.title: Schema-learning and rebinding as mechanisms of in-context learning and emergence
papers.research_question: How does in-context learning work, and can it be explained through schema-learning and rebinding mechanisms in interpretable models like clone-structured causal graphs (CSCGs)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that in-context learning can be achieved through schema-learning and rebinding mechanisms in interpretable clone-structured causal graphs, providing insights into how ICL works in large language models.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that schema-learning and rebinding mechanisms in CSCGs can explain in-context learning, offering insights for designing interpretable architectures and understanding emergence in large language models.
papers.key_findings:
CSCG achieves in-context learning on the GINC dataset, accurately retrieving latent concepts.
CSCG learns template circuits for algorithms and generalizes to novel tokens through rebinding on the LIALT dataset.
ICL performance improves with model overparameterization, suggesting emergence is related to capacity.
CSCG can inductively learn new word usage from single examples in the dax test.
The mechanisms of schema-learning and rebinding in CSCGs provide a plausible explanation for ICL in transformers.
papers.limitation:
CSCG fails to generalize to concepts unseen during training, similar to transformers.
Imperfections in learned CSCG models can lead to failure cases, such as wrong schema retrieval.
future_direction: Designing novel architectures based on schema-learning and rebinding principles.
Searching for interpretable and editable circuits in transformers using the identified mechanisms.
Extending the approach to more complex tasks and datasets.
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) is one of the most powerful and most unexpected capabilities to emerge in recent transformer-based large language models (LLMs). Yet the mechanisms that underlie it are poorly understood. In this paper, we demonstrate that comparable ICL capabilities can be acquired by an alternative sequence prediction learning method using clone-structured causal graphs (CSCGs). Moreover, a key property of CSCGs is that, unlike transformer-based LLMs, they are {\em interpretable}, which considerably simplifies the task of explaining how ICL works. Specifically, we show that it uses a combination of (a) learning template (schema) circuits for pattern completion, (b) retrieving relevant templates in a context-sensitive manner, and (c) rebinding of novel tokens to appropriate slots in the templates. We go on to marshall evidence for the hypothesis that similar mechanisms underlie ICL in LLMs. For example, we find that, with CSCGs as with LLMs, different capabilities emerge at different levels of overparameterization, suggesting that overparameterization helps in learning more complex template (schema) circuits. By showing how ICL can be achieved with small models and datasets, we open up a path to novel architectures, and take a vital step towards a more general understanding of the mechanics behind this important capability.

papers.title: Verifying Chain-of-Thought Reasoning via Its Computational Graph
papers.research_question: Does the computational graph of Chain-of-Thought reasoning steps contain structural fingerprints that distinguish correct from incorrect steps?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Circuit-based Reasoning Verification (CRV), a white-box method that uses structural fingerprints from attribution graphs to verify and correct Chain-of-Thought reasoning errors.
papers.conclusion: By analyzing the computational process of LLMs, CRV enables a deeper, causal understanding of reasoning failures, moving beyond simple error detection.
papers.key_findings:
Structural signatures of error in attribution graphs are highly predictive of reasoning correctness.
These signatures are domain-specific, with distinct computational patterns for different reasoning tasks.
The signatures are causal; targeted interventions on transcoder features can correct faulty reasoning.
CRV outperforms black-box and gray-box baselines in verification accuracy.
Error fingerprints are task-specific but can be combined in a multi-task classifier.
papers.limitation:
Computational intensity of CRV makes it impractical for real-time verification.
Aggregative feature analysis does not fully exploit semantic content of individual transcoder features.
Generalizability of error signatures across different model architectures and scales is unproven.
Fidelity of interpretability tools (transcoders, attribution methods) limits analysis resolution.
future_direction: Developing more sophisticated classifiers that operate on the semantics of transcoder features.
Studying generalizability of error signatures across model paradigms and scales.
Improving fidelity of interpretability tools for more precise analysis.
papers.abstract: Current Chain-of-Thought (CoT) verification methods predict reasoning correctness based on outputs (black-box) or activations (gray-box), but offer limited insight into why a computation fails. We introduce a white-box method: Circuit-based Reasoning Verification (CRV). We hypothesize that attribution graphs of correct CoT steps, viewed as execution traces of the model's latent reasoning circuits, possess distinct structural fingerprints from those of incorrect steps. By training a classifier on structural features of these graphs, we show that these traces contain a powerful signal of reasoning errors. Our white-box approach yields novel scientific insights unattainable by other methods. (1) We demonstrate that structural signatures of error are highly predictive, establishing the viability of verifying reasoning directly via its computational graph. (2) We find these signatures to be highly domain-specific, revealing that failures in different reasoning tasks manifest as distinct computational patterns. (3) We provide evidence that these signatures are not merely correlational; by using our analysis to guide targeted interventions on individual transcoder features, we successfully correct the model's faulty reasoning. Our work shows that, by scrutinizing a model's computational process, we can move from simple error detection to a deeper, causal understanding of LLM reasoning.

papers.title: Weight-of-Thought Reasoning: Exploring Neural Network Weights for Enhanced LLM Reasoning
papers.research_question: How can neural network weights be examined before inference to identify and enhance reasoning pathways in LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Weight-of-Thought reasoning, a novel approach that analyzes neural network weights prior to inference to identify and structure latent reasoning pathways, leading to improved performance and interpretability on complex reasoning tasks.
papers.conclusion: Weight-of-Thought reasoning represents a significant step toward more structured, efficient, and interpretable reasoning in neural networks by leveraging the weight space, offering a foundation for future research.
papers.key_findings:
WoT reasoning outperforms traditional methods like Chain-of-Thought on diverse reasoning tasks, especially complex multi-step problems.
The WoT model achieves superior performance with only ~2M parameters, demonstrating high parameter efficiency compared to large LLM baselines (~175B parameters).
Ablation studies show that weight-directed guidance, graph-based message passing, node specialization, and iterative refinement are all critical components contributing to WoT's performance.
Internal analysis reveals node specialization and dynamic, task-adaptive information flow within the reasoning graph.
WoT's graph structure enables parallel processing and adaptive information routing, moving beyond sequential reasoning chains.
papers.limitation:
Generalization capability across all types of reasoning problems requires further investigation.
The all-to-all message passing mechanism scales quadratically with the number of reasoning nodes, posing potential scaling challenges.
Performance is contingent on the quality and diversity of the training data.
Integrating WoT principles directly within the architecture of extremely large, pre-existing language models presents non-trivial technical hurdles.
Evaluation primarily relies on accuracy and MSE metrics, which may not fully encompass all facets of reasoning quality.
future_direction: Investigating generalization across broader reasoning problem types.
Addressing the quadratic scaling challenge of the message passing mechanism.
Developing integration techniques for large pre-existing language models and broader evaluation metrics.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable reasoning capabilities when prompted with strategies such as Chain-of-Thought (CoT).However, these approaches focus on token-level output without considering internal weight dynamics.We introduce Weight-of-Thought (WoT) reasoning, a novel approach that examines neural network weights before inference to identify reasoning pathways.Unlike existing methods, WoT explores the weight space through graph-based message passing, multi-step reasoning processes, and attention mechanisms.Our implementation creates an interconnected graph of reasoning nodes.Experiments on diverse reasoning tasks (syllogistic, mathematical, algebraic, combinatorial, and geometric) demonstrate that WoT achieves superior performance compared to traditional methods, particularly for complex problems.This approach leads to both improved performance and greater interpretability of the reasoning process, offering a promising direction for enhancing LLM reasoning capabilities.

papers.title: Latent Concept Disentanglement in Transformer-based Language Models
papers.research_question: How do transformers represent latent structures when performing in-context learning? Do they disentangle and compose latent concepts?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that transformers disentangle and compose latent concepts during in-context learning, representing them in low-dimensional subspaces that reflect the geometry of the latent parameters.
papers.conclusion: Transformers are capable of disentangling and composing latent concepts during in-context learning, with internal representations that capture the geometry of the underlying latent parameters.
papers.key_findings:
For multi-hop reasoning tasks, the model uses step-by-step composition of latent concepts via a sparse set of attention heads.
The bridge-resolving mechanism is much stronger in the larger 27B model compared to the 2B model, indicating model size benefits latent concept disentanglement.
Adding more in-context examples strengthens the causal importance of the relevant sub-circuits and increases concept representation disentanglement.
For numerical tasks with latent parameters, task vectors lie on low-dimensional smooth manifolds that reflect the geometry of the underlying parameter (e.g., radius).
Interpolating along the task vector manifold allows steering the model's computation, approximately interpolating the latent parameter.
papers.limitation:
Only English language queries are used, so mechanisms may differ across languages.
The latent concepts tested are all human-interpretable (e.g., numbers, countries), limiting generalization to more intricate relationships.
papers.abstract: When large language models (LLMs) use in-context learning (ICL) to solve a new task, they must infer latent concepts from demonstration examples. This raises the question of whether and how transformers represent latent structures as part of their computation. Our work experiments with several controlled tasks, studying this question using mechanistic interpretability. First, we show that in transitive reasoning tasks with a latent, discrete concept, the model successfully identifies the latent concept and does step-by-step concept composition. This builds upon prior work that analyzes single-step reasoning. Then, we consider tasks parameterized by a latent numerical concept. We discover low-dimensional subspaces in the model's representation space, where the geometry cleanly reflects the underlying parameterization. Overall, we show that small and large models can indeed disentangle and utilize latent concepts that they learn in-context from a handful of abbreviated demonstrations.

papers.title: A Closer Look at Bias and Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness of Large (Vision) Language Models
papers.research_question: Does chain-of-thought reasoning faithfully reflect model internal processes in large vision-language models? How do text-based and image-based biases affect reasoning and bias articulation?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a fine-grained evaluation pipeline for CoT faithfulness in LVLMs, finding that image-based biases are less articulated than text-based ones, and identifying inconsistent reasoning as a potential indicator of bias.
papers.conclusion: The study finds large variations in bias articulation rate depending on model training strategy and bias type, and identifies inconsistent reasoning as a failure mode. The 'reasonableness' of a bias affects articulation, and inconsistencies may signal biases in the absence of faithful CoTs.
papers.key_findings:
RL-trained reasoning models have substantially higher bias articulation rates compared to instruction-tuned or SFT-trained counterparts.
Visual biases are consistently less likely to be articulated than text-based biases, and subtle biases receive considerably less attention in model reasoning traces than explicit ones.
Models exhibit a previously unidentified phenomenon termed 'inconsistent reasoning' where they demonstrate correct reasoning before abruptly changing answers.
Inconsistent reasoning occurs more frequently when the bias conflicts with the ground truth, serving as a potential canary for detecting biased reasoning.
Bias articulation rates do not increase when given biased in-context samples, remaining constant across no-context, unbiased, and biased context settings.
papers.limitation:
They do not test faithfulness when inducing biases via training (as opposed to biased in-context samples).
They have yet to demonstrate detecting unfaithfulness when not explicit in the CoT in practical settings.
They do not have a theory to explain why some biases are articulated at a higher rate than others.
future_direction: Exploring faithfulness when inducing biases via training.
Demonstrating detection of unfaithfulness when not explicit in the CoT in practical settings.
Developing a theory to explain differences in bias articulation rates.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning enhances performance of large language models, but questions remain about whether these reasoning traces faithfully reflect the internal processes of the model. We present the first comprehensive study of CoT faithfulness in large vision-language models (LVLMs), investigating how both text-based and previously unexplored image-based biases affect reasoning and bias articulation. Our work introduces a novel, fine-grained evaluation pipeline for categorizing bias articulation patterns, enabling significantly more precise analysis of CoT reasoning than previous methods. This framework reveals critical distinctions in how models process and respond to different types of biases, providing new insights into LVLM CoT faithfulness. Our findings reveal that subtle image-based biases are rarely articulated compared to explicit text-based ones, even in models specialized for reasoning. Additionally, many models exhibit a previously unidentified phenomenon we term ``inconsistent'' reasoning - correctly reasoning before abruptly changing answers, serving as a potential canary for detecting biased reasoning from unfaithful CoTs. We then apply the same evaluation pipeline to revisit CoT faithfulness in LLMs across various levels of implicit cues. Our findings reveal that current language-only reasoning models continue to struggle with articulating cues that are not overtly stated.

papers.title: A Mechanistic Interpretation of Arithmetic Reasoning in Language Models using Causal Mediation Analysis
papers.research_question: How do language models process and store information related to arithmetic tasks? What model components are responsible for arithmetic reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Language models process arithmetic queries by transferring operand and operator information from early layers to the last token via attention, and then late MLP modules generate result-related information and incorporate it into the residual stream.
papers.conclusion: Causal mediation analysis reveals the mechanistic process of arithmetic reasoning in LMs, suggesting avenues for model pruning and targeted training.
papers.key_findings:
The model conveys operand and operator information from early layers to the last token using attention mechanisms.
Late MLP modules at the last token incorporate result-related information into the residual stream.
The activation patterns are specific to arithmetic queries compared to number retrieval and factual knowledge tasks.
The relative importance of late MLPs is high for arithmetic but low for other tasks.
Neuron-level interventions show that the top neurons for arithmetic overlap partially with number retrieval and not more than random with factual knowledge.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to the four fundamental arithmetic operators.
The queries are synthetically generated and not from real-life math word problems.
